analysis.one_liner: Makes it harder for workers to form small, targeted union bargaining units at their workplaces.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have raised the bar for forming small unions, died in committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Since a 2011 labor board ruling, small groups of workers—for example, nurses' aides at one facility—have been able to form their own bargaining unit even if coworkers in other departments stay out. This bill would reverse that, requiring the National Labor Relations Board to use a multi-factor test for whether workers share a 'sufficient community of interest' before approving a unit, which generally forces larger, harder-to-organize units. The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the Education and Workforce Committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers, particularly in labor-intensive service industries, benefit because the bill would make it much harder for small groups of employees to win union elections in small units, reducing both the number of organizing drives and the chance unions can organize a whole workplace piecemeal.

how_it_helps.text: It gives the NLRB an eight-factor test—wages, skills, supervision, work flow, and more—for deciding whether employees share a 'sufficient community of interest' before approving a bargaining unit.
It directs the Board to avoid 'proliferation or fragmentation' of bargaining units, barring separation of employees into their own unit unless their interests are sufficiently distinct.

analysis.who_pays: Workers who want to unionize, especially those in narrow job categories who would no longer be able to form small bargaining units, and unions that lose an organizing pathway.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers trying to organize small units

drawbacks.text: The bill would reinstate a standard that requires larger bargaining units, making it harder for small groups of employees—such as nurses' aides in one department or单个 store crews—to unionize at all, since many such groups would fail the 'sufficient community of interest' test.

The bill's factors lean on the employer's organizational structure and integration of the work flow, which can make it harder to organize any unit smaller than the whole workforce, the kind of unit the 2011 NLRB ruling explicitly allowed.

One concession: for accretions to existing units, the bill keeps the 'overwhelming community of interest' requirement and even tightens it by requiring new employees to have little or no separate identity.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stated rationale—preventing fragmented bargaining units and ensuring coherent bargaining—is a real policy argument, and larger units can make contracts less brittle. But the burden fell on workers seeking to organize small units, and the bill drew no Democratic support and died in committee without a hearing or vote, so no benefit was ever realized while the status quo it targeted remained.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: H.R. 2629 was introduced on May 24, 2017 by Rep. Francis Rooney with 10 Republican cosponsors and referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
The bill never advanced past that referral: no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action are recorded before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers opposed to micro-bargaining units are better off, since the legal standard the bill targeted remained unchanged only because the bill never moved—no action changed anything for either side.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers; the union-friendly micro-unit standard stayed intact

for.name: Rep. Francis Rooney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to reverse the NLRB's micro-unit standard.

for.name: 10 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did.

for.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
for.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill—it received no hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 10 cosponsors were Republicans and the bill sat untouched in the Republican-majority House; no Democratic support appears in the record.

industries.industry: Employers (especially retail, health care, and service-sector chains)
industries.note: The bill would make it harder for small groups of employees to form micro-unions, reducing the number of elections employers face and shrinking the risk of piecemeal organizing. This serves the employer's interest in avoiding unionization, which costs ordinary workers a channel for higher pay.
Unions have used micro-units to organize worksites where a majority of the whole workforce is out of reach. The bill would remove that pathway, cutting organizing opportunities.
